title: How We Got the New Testament
summary: Papyri, great codices, thousands of manuscripts, and the printed editions behind modern Bibles: what the differences between manuscripts are, what they do and do not change, and an honest answer to the claim that the Bible has been changed.

sections.h: From the first letters to the first copies
sections.body:
The books of the New Testament were written in Greek in the second half of the first century AD. Most were written for particular communities and read aloud when they arrived. Paul usually dictated his letters to a secretary and added a greeting in his own hand; one of those secretaries signs his name, “I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord” (Romans 16:22), and Paul points out his own handwriting at the end of Galatians and 2 Thessalonians. The Gospels were written for wider circulation. Copies were made almost at once: Paul asks the Colossians to pass their letter to Laodicea and read the one sent there (Colossians 4:16), and a church that received a letter from an apostle would want its own copy, and neighboring churches would want theirs.

The original documents, which scholars call the autographs, have all perished, as have the originals of every ancient book. Papyrus, the common writing material, lasts a long time only in very dry conditions, which is why most early biblical papyri come from Egypt. What survives are copies. From a very early date Christians preferred the codex, a book of folded sheets stitched at the spine, to the scroll that Jews and pagans used for literature. The codex was cheaper, since it used both sides of the sheet, easier to carry, and easier to search, and it could hold all four Gospels or all of Paul's letters in one volume. Nearly all early Christian manuscripts are codices.

The earliest copyists were often not professional scribes but literate believers, copying for their own congregations, and the earliest papyri show a range of skill from careful to careless. As the church grew and, after the conversion of Constantine in the early fourth century, gained resources, professional copying in scriptoria produced large, handsome Bibles. In the Byzantine centuries, monasteries produced thousands of copies in a standardized form. Every copy was made by hand until the invention of printing in the fifteenth century, and every hand-made copy differs from every other in some small ways. That is the root of the whole subject.

sections.h: The manuscripts: how many and what kinds
sections.body:
Greek manuscripts of the New Testament are catalogued by the Institute for New Testament Textual Research (INTF) in Münster, Germany, in a register called the Kurzgefasste Liste, and they are known by the numbers assigned in that system (the Gregory-Aland numbers). They fall into four groups. Papyri are manuscripts written on papyrus, numbered with a P and a superscript; there are about 140, most from the second to the fourth centuries and most fragmentary. Majuscules (also called uncials) are parchment manuscripts written in capital letters, numbered with a zero first (01, 02, and so on) and, for the famous ones, a letter; there are over three hundred, mostly from the fourth to the tenth centuries. Minuscules, written in a joined lowercase hand that came into use in the ninth century, are the largest group, nearly three thousand. Lectionaries, books arranging passages for reading in church through the year, number around 2,500.

The usual headline figure, repeated in many books, is that there are more than 5,800 Greek manuscripts; Daniel Wallace of the Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts reported a count of 5,838 catalogued items in 2013, and the catalog has grown since. That figure counts catalog numbers, not surviving books. In a chapter of Myths and Mistakes in New Testament Textual Criticism (edited by Elijah Hixson and Peter Gurry, 2019), Jacob Peterson showed that some numbers refer to manuscripts that are lost, destroyed, or turned out to be parts of other manuscripts already counted, and he proposed that about 5,300 Greek manuscripts actually exist, with 5,100 the safer figure. Most are also partial: only a few dozen contain the whole New Testament, and many contain only the Gospels. The honest number is smaller than the slogan, and it is still enormous.

Besides Greek manuscripts, textual critics use early translations (versions) and quotations by early Christian writers. The New Testament was translated into Latin, Syriac, and Coptic by the third century, and later into Armenian, Georgian, Ethiopic, Gothic, and other languages; there are thousands of Latin manuscripts alone. The church fathers from the second century on quoted the New Testament constantly in sermons, commentaries, and letters, and their quotations show what text was read in a particular place and time, though fathers often quoted loosely or from memory, so their evidence has to be weighed with care.

No other ancient text comes close to this abundance or earliness of evidence. Popular apologetics sometimes overstates the comparison with classical authors such as Homer, Plato, or Tacitus, by using outdated counts for the classics or treating tiny fragments as whole books, and the Myths and Mistakes volume corrects several of these claims. The corrected comparison still leaves the New Testament far ahead: a copy of the Gospels or Paul's letters within about 150 years of their writing is not unusual for it and almost unheard of for any classical work.

sections.body:
A handful of manuscripts carry disproportionate weight because of their age or quality. The earliest is P52, a scrap about the size of a credit card in the John Rylands Library in Manchester, with parts of John 18:31-33 on one side and 18:37-38 on the other. When C. H. Roberts published it in 1935 he dated it on the basis of its handwriting to the first half of the second century, often cited as around 125. Brent Nongbri (Harvard Theological Review, 2005) showed that handwriting comparisons allow a wider range, including the later second and even early third century, and many papyrologists now give a broader date. It remains among the earliest surviving pieces of the New Testament.

The great papyrus books come from around AD 200. P46, part of the Chester Beatty collection (Dublin and Ann Arbor), contains most of Paul's letters and Hebrews. P66 and P75, in the Bodmer collection (P75 is now in the Vatican Library), contain much of John, and in P75's case much of Luke as well. P75's text is remarkably close to that of Codex Vaticanus, copied perhaps 150 years later; their agreement in Luke and John is over 90 percent by most counts, which showed that the kind of text in Vaticanus was not a fourth-century scholarly revision but reached back at least to the late second century.

The great parchment Bibles come from the fourth and fifth centuries. Codex Sinaiticus (01 or Aleph), from the mid-fourth century, is the oldest complete New Testament; the German scholar Constantin von Tischendorf saw leaves of it at Saint Catherine's Monastery at Mount Sinai in 1844 and obtained most of the rest in 1859, in circumstances the monastery has long disputed. Most of it was sold by the Soviet government to the British Museum in 1933 and is now in the British Library. Codex Vaticanus (03 or B), also fourth century, has been in the Vatican Library since at least the fifteenth century; it lacks the end of Hebrews, the Pastoral Letters, Philemon, and Revelation. Codex Alexandrinus (02 or A), from the fifth century, was given to King Charles I of England in 1627 by Cyril Lucaris, Patriarch of Constantinople. Codex Bezae (05 or D), from around 400, has Greek and Latin on facing pages and a text full of striking additions and differences, especially in Acts; the Reformer Theodore Beza gave it to Cambridge University in 1581.

sections.h: How the differences arose and how critics weigh them
sections.body:
When scholars compare manuscripts, they find that the differences cluster into families. The Alexandrian text, found in P75, Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, and many Egyptian witnesses, tends to be shorter and plainer. The so-called Western text, found in Codex Bezae, the Old Latin, and some early fathers, is freer, with paraphrases and additions, especially in Acts. The Byzantine text, found in the great majority of later manuscripts, is smoother and fuller; it tends to harmonize parallel passages and combine alternative readings, and it became the standard text of the Greek church. Many scholars now treat these ‘text types’ as loose tendencies rather than sharply defined families.

Most differences arose by accident. A scribe's eye skipped a line between two words with the same ending. Letters were misread, especially in continuous capital script without spaces between words. Words were spelled in the way the scribe pronounced them. Some changes were intentional but well meant: a scribe harmonized a saying in Mark with its form in Matthew, completed a quotation of the Old Testament, added ‘Jesus’ where the text said ‘he’, or clarified what seemed ambiguous. A small number reflect theological concerns, which Bart Ehrman studied in The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture (1993), arguing that scribes of the second and third centuries sometimes altered texts to guard against views they considered heretical.

Textual critics decide between readings with two kinds of evidence. External evidence asks about the manuscripts: how old are those that support each reading, how widely spread geographically, and how reliable are they elsewhere? Internal evidence asks about the reading itself: which reading best explains how the others arose? Which would a scribe be more likely to change than to create? Other things being equal, critics prefer the more difficult reading, since scribes tended to smooth difficulties, and often the shorter reading, since scribes more often added than cut, though that rule has many exceptions. Most modern scholars practice a ‘reasoned eclecticism’ that weighs both kinds of evidence; Bruce Metzger's A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament explains the committee's decision for each significant passage in the standard edition.

Since the 1990s the INTF has used a computer-assisted method called the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method (CBGM), developed by Gerd Mink, to map the relationships among manuscripts in far greater detail. It underlies the Editio Critica Maior, a vast critical edition published book by book, beginning with the Catholic Letters. The ECM's editors speak of reconstructing the ‘initial text’, the earliest text recoverable from the surviving tradition, and they are candid that in some places they cannot decide between readings; such places are marked in the edition.

sections.h: Printed editions: from Erasmus to Nestle-Aland
sections.body:
The first printed Greek New Testament to be published was the edition of the Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus, issued in Basel in 1516 under the title Novum Instrumentum omne. (The Complutensian Polyglot, prepared in Spain under Cardinal Ximenes, printed its New Testament in 1514 but was not released until the early 1520s.) Erasmus worked quickly from a handful of late Byzantine manuscripts available in Basel; for Revelation he had only one manuscript, which lacked the last six verses, and he supplied them by translating the Latin Vulgate back into Greek. He revised the text in later editions, and in the third (1522) he added the words about the three heavenly witnesses in 1 John 5:7-8, which he had omitted earlier because he found them in no Greek manuscript.

Later editions by the Paris printer Robert Estienne (Stephanus), especially his royal edition of 1550, the first with a critical apparatus, and his 1551 edition, the first with verse numbers, and by Theodore Beza in Geneva, built on Erasmus. In 1633 the Elzevir printers of Leiden advertised their edition as the text now received by all, and the phrase gave this family of editions its name, the Textus Receptus (‘received text’). The King James translators of 1611 used editions of this kind.

As older manuscripts came to light, scholars gathered their readings. John Mill's edition of 1707 listed about 30,000 differences among the manuscripts known to him, which alarmed some readers then as similar numbers alarm some now. Karl Lachmann's edition of 1831 was the first to abandon the Textus Receptus and build a text from the oldest witnesses. Tischendorf's eighth edition (1869 to 1872) and the edition of Brooke Foss Westcott and Fenton John Anthony Hort, The New Testament in the Original Greek (1881), relying heavily on Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, laid the foundation of modern critical texts. Eberhard Nestle's handy edition of 1898 became, through the work of Kurt and Barbara Aland and others, the Nestle-Aland Novum Testamentum Graece, now in its twenty-eighth edition (2012); the United Bible Societies' Greek New Testament (fifth edition, 2014) has the same text with an apparatus designed for translators. The twenty-eighth edition revised the Catholic Letters in light of the Editio Critica Maior, and a twenty-ninth edition, drawing on the ECM for further books, has been announced. Other modern editions include the SBL Greek New Testament (2010, edited by Michael Holmes) and The Greek New Testament produced at Tyndale House, Cambridge (2017, edited by Dirk Jongkind, Peter Williams, and colleagues).

Not all scholars accept the priority given to the earliest manuscripts. The Byzantine-priority view, represented by Maurice Robinson and William Pierpont's edition of the Byzantine Textform (2005), holds that the text found in the majority of manuscripts best preserves the original, as does the earlier Majority Text edition of Zane Hodges and Arthur Farstad (1982). Others, including the Trinitarian Bible Society, defend the Textus Receptus itself as the providentially preserved text. The New King James Version (1982) translates the Textus Receptus and footnotes differences from the critical and majority texts. Most translations since the Revised Version of 1881 are based on the critical text.

sections.h: The passages a reader will notice
sections.body:
Most variants make no difference a reader of an English Bible could see. A few do, and modern Bibles mark them with brackets or footnotes. The two longest are passages of twelve verses each. The ending of Mark after 16:8 (Mark 16:9-20) is absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and several early writers note that the best copies they knew ended at 16:8; other manuscripts have a short ending of a sentence or two, or both endings. Yet the longer ending was known in the second century, since Irenaeus quotes Mark 16:19 around 180, and it stands in the great majority of manuscripts. Most scholars conclude it was added early to supply an ending, and debate whether Mark meant to end at 16:8 or whether an original ending was lost; a minority, including Maurice Robinson and Nicholas Lunn (The Original Ending of Mark, 2014), argue that it is original. The story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus, first appears in a Greek manuscript in Codex Bezae, and in some manuscripts stands after John 7:36, John 21:25, or Luke 21:38. Many scholars who think it was not part of John's Gospel nonetheless regard it as an early and credible tradition about Jesus. The BSB, like most modern translations, prints both passages with a note.

Several shorter passages are also well known. The words about three witnesses in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, which the King James Version includes at 1 John 5:7-8 (the Johannine Comma), arose in Latin and appear in only a handful of late Greek manuscripts, some of them only in the margin; no modern critical edition includes them, and the doctrine of the Trinity was confessed at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) without them. Luke 22:43-44, the angel strengthening Jesus and his sweat like drops of blood, is missing from P75 and Vaticanus but present in Sinaiticus and Bezae, and Justin Martyr in the second century seems to know it; scholars are genuinely divided. In Luke 23:34 the prayer “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” is also missing from P75 and Vaticanus; many scholars nonetheless think it belongs to Luke's Gospel, or at least preserves a genuine saying of Jesus, and the BSB prints it. The doxology at the end of the Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6:13, the confession of the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:37, and the angel stirring the water in John 5:4 are absent from the earliest witnesses; the BSB and most modern translations leave them out of the text and give them in footnotes, which is why some verse numbers seem to be missing (see Chapters, Verses, and References).

Other variants affect a single word. In Mark 1:41, nearly all manuscripts say Jesus was ‘moved with compassion’ when a leper asked for healing, but Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies say he was ‘angry’; the NIV of 2011 adopted ‘indignant’, while the BSB and most others keep compassion. In Hebrews 2:9, almost all manuscripts say Jesus tasted death for everyone ‘by the grace of God’, but a few manuscripts and some early writers, including Origen, knew a reading ‘apart from God’, which Ehrman and some others argue is original. In John 1:18 the earliest manuscripts read ‘the one and only God’ (monogenēs theos), later ones ‘the only begotten Son’. In 1 Timothy 3:16 later manuscripts read ‘God was manifested in the flesh’ where earlier ones read ‘who was manifested’. In Romans 5:1, the difference of one letter decides between ‘we have peace with God’ and ‘let us have peace with God’, and most translators choose the first on grounds of sense though the second is better attested.

sections.h: Has the Bible been changed? The case as Ehrman makes it
sections.body:
The strongest popular form of the objection comes from Bart Ehrman, a respected textual critic at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Ehrman grew up an evangelical, studied at Moody Bible Institute and Wheaton College, and wrote his doctorate at Princeton Theological Seminary under Bruce Metzger, the leading American textual critic of his generation, with whom he later revised Metzger's standard handbook (The Text of the New Testament, fourth edition, 2005). His book Misquoting Jesus: The Story Behind Who Changed the Bible and Why (2005) became a bestseller and brought textual criticism to a wide audience for the first time.

The argument deserves to be stated as its author would state it. We do not have the originals of any New Testament book. We have copies made years, decades, and in most cases centuries later, and the copies differ from one another. Scholars estimate the number of variants in the hundreds of thousands; Ehrman cited estimates as high as 400,000, more than the number of words in the Greek New Testament (about 138,000). Most variants are insignificant, as Ehrman himself says, but some matter: whether Jesus was angry or compassionate in Mark 1:41, whether he was calm or in anguish before his arrest in Luke 22:43-44, whether he died ‘apart from God’ in Hebrews 2:9. Whole passages, such as the ending of Mark and the woman caught in adultery, were not in the earliest copies. Some changes were made deliberately by scribes with theological motives. And the earliest period, when the text was copied most freely by non-professionals, is the period for which we have the least evidence. If God inspired the very words of the originals, Ehrman asks, why did he not preserve them? For a Christian who believes the Bible is inerrant in its autographs, he argues, the fact that we do not have those autographs and cannot recover them with certainty everywhere is a serious problem.

Ehrman tells in the book's introduction how his study of the manuscripts, beginning with a seminary paper on the problem of Abiathar in Mark 2:26, unsettled his belief in inerrancy. He is now an agnostic, but he has written that textual criticism was not what finally took his faith; in God's Problem (2008) he explains that it was the problem of suffering. That distinction matters. The question of the text is a historical question, and it can be answered on historical grounds.

Everything factual in this summary is accurate, and a Christian reader should not pretend otherwise. The originals are lost; the copies differ; the numbers are large; some scribes did change texts on purpose; some well-loved passages were probably not in the first copies. The question is what follows.

sections.h: The replies, and where the evidence leaves us
sections.body:
The first reply concerns the numbers. A variant is any place where any manuscript differs from the others, and each manuscript's deviation is counted, so the number of variants grows with the number of manuscripts. A large number is the result of abundant evidence, not of a bad text; a book surviving in one copy would have no variants at all and far less certainty. Peter Gurry, in a 2016 study in New Testament Studies, proposed that the true figure is about 500,000 variants, not counting spelling differences, higher than earlier estimates. The number does not frighten textual critics because of what the variants are.

That is the second reply. Daniel Wallace, who debated Ehrman publicly in New Orleans in 2008 (published as The Reliability of the New Testament: Bart D. Ehrman and Daniel B. Wallace in Dialogue, edited by Robert Stewart, 2011), sorts variants into four kinds. The great majority are spelling and nonsense errors that affect nothing. Next are differences that cannot be translated, such as word order (Greek word order is flexible) or whether a proper name has the article. Then come variants that would change meaning but have no real chance of being original, because they appear in one late manuscript. The fourth kind, variants that are both meaningful and viable, is by Wallace's count less than one percent of the total. These are the passages discussed above, and they are printed in the footnotes of every good English Bible.

The third reply concerns what the meaningful variants touch. No doctrine of the creeds depends on a disputed reading. The deity of Christ does not rest on 1 John 5:7 or 1 Timothy 3:16; it is taught in passages whose text is secure (John 1:1, John 20:28, Philippians 2:5-11, Hebrews 1). Jesus' anguish in Gethsemane is in Mark 14:32-42 whatever is decided about Luke 22:43-44. Ehrman himself, in an interview printed in some editions of Misquoting Jesus, said that his position does not stand at odds with Metzger's view that the essential Christian beliefs are not affected by the textual variants. Timothy Paul Jones's Misquoting Truth (2007), the first book-length response, and the essays in Myths and Mistakes (2019) make the related point that the variants reveal a tradition that can be checked, because the evidence is abundant and early.

The replies also correct overstatements on the Christian side. Myths and Mistakes was written in part to stop apologists from inflating manuscript counts, redating papyri to the first century on thin grounds. Textual critics working in the Editio Critica Maior acknowledge places where the evidence is so evenly balanced that they print a split reading. The New Testament text is not certain in every word. It is certain in the vast majority of its words, and where it is uncertain, the uncertainty is visible, bounded, and marked.

Where does that leave the question of inspiration? Christians have always confessed that God inspired the original writings, and the doctrine has never depended on any single manuscript being perfect. Evangelical textual critics such as Wallace argue that the ‘initial text’ recoverable from the manuscripts is, in all but a small number of words, the text the authors wrote, and that God's providence is shown in the abundance of the witnesses rather than in any single perfect copy. Ehrman and others reply that ‘all but a small number’ still leaves real gaps. A reader can weigh that exchange fairly. What cannot fairly be said is that the church has hidden the evidence, or that the New Testament was rewritten beyond recognition. The manuscripts are public, catalogued, photographed, and increasingly online, and the variants are printed at the bottom of the page.
